highlights:
Authentication | Pylon

# Authentication

How to authenticate with Pylon's API

The Pylon API uses Bearer authentication. This means you’ll need to pass your API token in the header of your request:

```
Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

Generate an API token in the Pylon dashboard.

### API regions

Pylon’s API is available in two regions. Use the base URL that matches where your Pylon tenant is hosted:

- US region: https://api.usepylon.com
- EU region: https://api.eu.usepylon.com

Both regions use the same API endpoints and authentication. Configure your integration to use the region where your Pylon tenant is hosted.

You can tell a token's region from its prefix:

| Prefix | Region |
| --- | --- |
| `pylon_api_eu_` | EU |
| `pylon_api_` | US |

Tokens created before prefixes were introduced have no prefix. Sending a token to the other region's API returns `401` with the `wrong_region_token` error code, and the message names the correct URL.

Once you've created a token, call the `/me` endpoint to retrieve details about your organization and confirm your token works.

## Create an API token

Only Admins can create and manage API tokens.

1. Go to Settings > Integrations & dev > API. On the Tokens tab, click Create API Token.
2. Enter a Name.
3. Choose who the token acts as:

- Leave Act as user or bot (optional) empty to give the token its own identity. Pick a Role to control what it can access, and optionally upload an icon.
- Or select a teammate or bot. The token uses that user's current role and permissions.
4. Optionally, add an IP allowlist (see below).
5. Click Create and copy the token. Pylon shows it only once.

Tokens don't expire, and their access is controlled only by the role. There are no separate scopes.

### Roles

A token with its own identity uses the role you pick when you create it. You can change the role later with Edit. Older tokens that have no role act as Admin.

A token that acts as a user or bot has no role of its own. It always uses that user's current role, so changing the user's role changes what the token can do.

See Roles and user management for what each role allows.

### Who actions are attributed to

- Token with its own identity: actions show up under the token's name and icon.
- Token that acts as a user or bot: actions are attributed to that user or bot.

### Bots

Bots are identities for automation, so API activity is attributed to the bot instead of to a teammate. Bots can't sign in to Pylon.

To create one, go to Settings > Workspace > Users, open the Bots tab, and click New Bot. Give it a name, an avatar, and a role. Then select the bot under Act as user or bot when you create a token.

### IP allowlist

Add IP addresses (for example `203.0.113.10`) or CIDR blocks (for example `203.0.113.0/24`) to restrict where the token can be used. You can add up to 20 entries. If the list is empty, the token works from any IP.

Pylon checks the public IP address your requests come from, so add the public egress IPs or ranges of the servers that call the API. Private addresses such as `10.0.0.0/8` or `192.168.0.0/16` never match.

A request from an address that isn't on the list returns `401` with the `invalid_api_token` error code.

## Manage tokens

The Tokens tab shows each token's Acts as, Token preview, Role, Created by, Last used, and Created values. From the … menu on a token you can:

- Edit: change the name, role, or IP allowlist.
- Duplicate Token: create a new token with the same settings.
- Rotate: generate a new token value. The current token stops working immediately.
- Delete: permanently revoke the token. Calls using it stop working immediately.
- View Activity: open the token's request logs.

## Review API request logs

Only Admins can view request logs. Go to Settings > Integrations & dev > API and open the Logs tab, or choose View Activity from a token's … menu to see only that token's requests.

Filter by token, or choose All tokens, and by a date range of up to 90 days. The range defaults to the last 7 days. Each request shows when it was made, the token, who it acted as, the method, endpoint, response status, source IP, user agent, and request ID. Requests made with a token that was since deleted still appear.

Requests rejected for authentication or rate limits aren't logged, and older requests may not show a token.

### When tokens are revoked automatically

When a user is deactivated, Pylon deletes:

- every API token that user created, and
- every API token that acts as that user.

Before you deactivate someone who created tokens your integrations rely on, create replacement tokens from another Admin's account.

An Admin who has created Admin-role tokens can't be moved to a different role until those tokens are deleted.

highlights:
# How do I create a Pylon API token?

 Last updated 2 months ago 

Applies to: Pylon API access

To create a Pylon API token, sign in as a user with permission to manage API tokens, then open Settings → API Tokens. If you do not see that page, ask a workspace admin to create the token or update your access.

1. Open Settings → API Tokens.
2. Select Create.
3. Enter a token name, then finish creation.
4. Copy the token immediately and store it in a secure location. Pylon only shows the full token value once.

Use the token to authenticate Pylon API requests with a Bearer header:

- `Authorization: Bearer <token>`

If you need read-only access, a workspace admin should choose an appropriate role for the token when creating it.

auth.title: API Reference - Pylon
highlights:
API root URL 

```bash
https://api.getpylon.com
```

#  Authentication 

 To start making requests to the API, you'll need to first create an API token in your API settings area. You can create multiple tokens, and revoke them at any time. Tokens are associated with your team and the user who created them. 

 Pass your API token in the `Authorization` header as shown in the example, where `$TOKEN` should be replaced with your actual secret API token value. You should always use HTTPS when making requests containing sensitive information, and our API will return an error if you use a non-HTTPS URL. 

## API token security

 Your API token is intended for server-side use, and should not be distributed to browsers (e.g. in page HTML or in a JavaScript bundle), nor committed to source control. If you suspect a token has been compromised, revoke it immediately from your API settings. 

 Do not distribute API tokens using emails, SMS messages, or group chat software. Doing this leaves your API token in history from where it could be leaked. If you need to transmit API tokens between team members or to third parties (e.g. your IT contractor), use a secure ephemeral service. This instance of SnapPass provides such a service. 

 Delete unused API keys, and keys created for development or testing purposes, to reduce the chance of a leak. Consider regenerating API keys periodically by creating a new key, switching your applications to it, then deleting the old key. Our API logging helps you ensure that you have switched completely before deleting the old key. 

## Permissions

 When you create an API token to make requests with, you can assign it permissions. By creating multiple tokens with appropriate permissions, you can increase the security of your integration. 

| Permission | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `read` | This permission allows reading any data which is in your account. This includes sensitive customer and business information, so be extremely careful who you give `read` API tokens to. |
| `write` | This is required in order to create new resources, but does not grant the ability to update any existing resources. This protects the integrity of your account data. |
| `update` | This is required in order to update existing resources. It may often need to be paired with the `read` permission to enable automated workflows. |
| `payment` | This permission is required for any billable API calls, as well as API calls which may spend your Pylon credit balance. |

 Authenticated request 

```bash
curl https://api.getpylon.com/v1/users \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --header "Accept: application/vnd.api+json"
```

...

### Content types

 When making requests to resource endpoints, your client should specify the `Accept: application/vnd.api+json` request header. In addition, requests with bodies (e.g. POST, PATCH) should include the header `Content-Type: application/vnd.api+json`.

highlights:
## Authentication Types

Pylon supports 1 authentication method:

- API Key - Use a token generated in the Pylon dashboard for all API requests
- Pros: Quick setup, simple configuration, no OAuth app creation needed
- Cons: Single token for all users, no per-user tracking, actions appear as the token name

## Setting up API Key

1. Navigate to https://app.usepylon.com/settings/api-tokens
2. Click Create Token
3. Enter a name for the token (e.g., "Willow Integration")
4. Copy the generated API token immediately

:::warning
Keep your API token secure! Never share it publicly or commit it to version control. Anyone with this token has full access to your Pylon workspace.
:::

1. In Willow, go to Integrations → New → Built-in
2. Select Pylon and click Use
3. Select API Key as the authentication method
4. Paste your API token into the token field
5. Click Save to complete the setup

### Verify the Connection

After saving, you can test the connection by using the Get Me tool. It should return your organization details, confirming the token is valid.

Frequently asked questions

How is Pylon priced?

Pylon is priced based on the number of seats and the number of agentic credits your team needs. Because B2B support teams vary significantly in size and workflow, pricing reflects your team's unique needs. Book a demo and we'll put together a quote specific to your setup.

Is pricing per seat, per ticket, or per account?

Pylon's pricing is seat-based and credit usage-based. You're not charged per ticket, so your costs stay predictable as your customer base grows, even as ticket volume scales.

What's included in every plan?

Every plan includes core ticketing, unified ticketing (Slack, email, and chat widget), omnichannel support, a knowledge base, NPS and CSAT surveys, and analytics.

Are AI features included, or are they a separate add-on?

...

Does Pylon offer annual and monthly billing, and is there a discount for paying annually?

Pylon offers both annual and monthly billing. When you commit to credits upfront, you will receive a discount.

Do I have to buy credits upfront?

No. Pylon offers both pay-as-you-go credits and committed credit plans, so teams can buy credits as they need them or commit upfront. You can purchase additional credits in-product anytime.

Is there a minimum seat requirement or minimum contract size?

There is a minimum seat count for new customers. Pylon is built for B2B support teams rather than solo operators, so it's designed to deliver value at team scale.

What does a contract with Pylon look like?

Standard contracts are annual. Multi-year agreements are available for teams that want rate lock and additional flexibility. Credits can be used across the entire contract term and buying more at once will result in a higher credit discount.

What counts as a "seat"?

A seat covers any teammate who needs to work tickets, including agents and admins with inbox access. Stakeholders who only need visibility into conversations, without working them, can use a viewer seat.

Do you have viewer seats?

Yes, Pylon has view-only seats. Your sales representative will work with you on the number of viewer seats your team needs.

Does Pylon offer a free trial or free plan?

Pylon offers free trials for prospects. Your sales representative will work with you on setting up the demo organization.

Is there a minimum number of accounts required for Account Intelligence?

Yes. Account Intelligence requires a minimum of 50 customer accounts.

mcp.title: Pylon MCP | Pylon
highlights:
# Pylon MCP

Expose Pylon data to AI tools and assistants via Model Context Protocol.

## Pylon MCP Server

The Pylon MCP Server exposes Pylon data to AI tools that support the Model Context Protocol (e.g. Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor). AI tools authenticate with OAuth or an API token and can read and update issues, accounts, contacts, knowledge base articles, tasks and projects, triggers, and more within the authenticated identity's permissions.

- Server URL (US): `https://mcp.usepylon.com`
- Server URL (EU): `https://mcp.eu.usepylon.com`
- Auth: OAuth 2.0 or an API token. Actions are performed as the signed-in user or the token's identity, with that identity's current role and permissions.
- Transport: Streamable HTTP (stateless; no server-side sessions).

### Setup in Pylon

Open Settings > AI Controls > MCP Server in Pylon. Copy your workspace's regional MCP URL from Installation and use it in your AI tool. For client-specific instructions, see connecting to the Pylon MCP Server.

### Authentication

Both methods use the same regional MCP URL. Choose the method your client supports.

#### OAuth

Use OAuth with AI tools that offer an interactive connection flow. Add the regional MCP URL to your client, then sign in to Pylon when prompted. MCP requests run as the user who authorizes the connection.

#### API token

Use an existing API token for headless workers, scripts, or MCP clients that support custom authorization headers. You don't need a separate MCP token or an interactive sign-in.

1. Create or choose an API token.
2. Configure your client with your workspace's regional MCP URL.
3. Include this header on every MCP request:

Replace `<API_TOKEN>` with the token value. Use `https://mcp.usepylon.com` for US workspaces and `https://mcp.eu.usepylon.com` for EU workspaces; the token must belong to the same region.

A token with its own identity uses the role assigned to that identity. A token linked to a teammate or bot uses that user's current role and permissions. The identity must have MCP Access, and each tool still requires the permissions for its operation. Any IP allowlist configured on the token also applies to MCP requests.

Some clients only support OAuth connections. Use their OAuth flow if they don't let you configure an authorization header.

### What you can do with MCP today

The authenticated user or token identity needs the MCP Access permission to connect. The standard Member and Admin roles include this permission. Each tool also requires the permissions for its operation. Access follows the same scoping as the Pylon dashboard — the MCP cannot return data that the authenticated user cannot already see, or perform writes that the authenticated user cannot already write in the UI.

Some tools also require a plan feature, noted in their section. Rate limits apply per tool, elaborated below.

Use the tool names below when configuring your AI client. Your client discovers the input schema for each tool through MCP; available tools depend on your workspace, plan, and permissions.

For a tool whose input schema includes `arguments`, put its required and optional fields inside that object. For example:

Use the schema returned by your client for the exact fields. Writes apply immediately; confirm the intended change before calling them. If the outcome of a write is unknown, check the record before retrying.

Write tools reject arguments they don't recognize instead of ignoring them; the error names the unknown arguments and lists the valid ones. A different casing of a field name, such as `customerPortalTitle` for `customer_portal_title`, is accepted, and tools with a `state` field also accept `status`. Supply each field only once: sending a field under both its name and an alias returns an error.

#### Issues

AI tools can send replies to customers and post internal notes for your team. A reply goes straight to the customer on the issue's channel (Slack, email, chat, etc.) and can't be unsent, so AI tools are instructed to show you the exact message and get your approval before sending it. Most AI tools also ask you to confirm each reply.

| Tool | Read / Write | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `search_issues` | Read | Search issues by keyword (titles, messages, tags, and names) and by state, account, assignee, tags, custom fields, etc. Each result lists its linked engineering tickets and their state |
| `get_issue` | Read | Fetch a single issue by ID or number; set `include_messages=true` to include its conversation |
| `get_issue_messages` | Read | Fetch an issue's full message history in order, including the original To and Cc recipients of email messages and each message's attachments |
| `get_message_attachment` | Read | Fetch one attachment from an issue message |
| `get_issue_statuses` | Read | List the default and custom issue statuses configured for your organization |
| `create_issue` | Write | Create an issue in your workspace with an initial internal note |
| `update_issue` | Write | Update issue fields (status, assignee, team, priority, tags, custom fields, …); tags can be replaced or added and removed individually |
| `update_issues` | Write | Apply the same status, assignee, team, or tag change to up to 100 issues in one call |
| `snooze_issue` | Write | Snooze an issue until a future time. It moves to On hold and returns to Waiting on you when the snooze ends |
| `send_issue_reply` | Write | Send a reply to the customer on an issue. For email issues, recipients follow reply-all |
| `send_issue_note` | Write | Post an internal note on an issue, visible only to your team |
| `get_issue_threads` | Read | List an issue's internal threads |
| `create_issue_thread` | Write | Create an internal thread on an issue, optionally synced to an internal Slack channel |
| `get_issue_followers` | Read | List an issue's followers |
| `update_issue_followers` | Write | Add or remove teammates as followers of an issue |
| `link_product_issue` | Write | Link a Linear, Jira, GitHub, Asana, or Shortcut ticket to an issue |
| `add_issue_group_children` | Write | Add children to an issue group |
| `create_issue_ai_response` | Write | Create an AI response for an issue |
| `create_issue_group` | Write | Create an issue group |
| `delete_issue` | Write | Delete an existing issue |
| `delete_message` | Write | Delete a message |
| `get_issue_voice_calls` | Read | Get voice calls (with recordings and transcripts) for an issue |
| `link_external_incident` | Write | Link or unlink an incident to/from an issue |
| `mark_issues_as_spam` | Write | Mark issues as spam |
| `merge_issues` | Write | Merge issues |
| `redact_message` | Write | Redact a message |
| `remove_issue_group_child` | Write | Remove a child from an issue group |
| `update_message` | Write | Edit a message |

`search_issues` can return each issue's messages with `include_messages`. ... Set `include_total` to also get the exact number of matching issues you can read across

...

#### Knowledge Base

Reading requires permission to view the knowledge base. Drafting, publishing, changing article settings and tags, and editing collections require the same edit and publish permissions as the Pylon knowledge base editor.

| Tool | Read / Write | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `list_knowledge_bases` | Read | List the knowledge bases you can read |
| `list_collections` | Read | List collections in a knowledge base |
| `get_collection` | Read | Fetch a collection's details and visibility settings |
| `list_collection_contents` | Read | List the articles and sub-collections directly inside a collection |
| `save_collection` | Write | Create a collection, or edit an existing collection's title, description, or slug, or move it under another collection |
| `search_articles` | Read | Full-text search across article titles and content |
| `get_article` | Read | Fetch an article's content, visibility settings, and tags, by ID or by the identifier in its public URL; optionally include its images |

...

#### Tasks & Projects

Requires Account Intelligence.

| Tool | Read / Write | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `search_tasks` | Read | Search tasks across your organization, or for one account or project |
| `get_task` | Read | Fetch a task, including its subtasks and 20 most recent comments |
| `get_task_statuses` | Read | List the default and custom task statuses |
| `save_task` | Write | Create a task or update only the fields you provide |

...

#### REST API

When no other tool does what you need, AI tools can run operations from the Pylon REST API directly. Each call runs as the authenticated user, so the operation's own permission checks apply, just as they do in the Pylon dashboard.

| Tool | Read / Write | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `search_api_operations` | Read | Find REST API operations by keyword, and the named tool that runs each one |
| `get_api_operation` | Read | Get an operation's argument schema and response shape |

An AI tool finds an operation with `search_api_operations`, gets its arguments with `get_api_operation`, then runs it with the named tool returned as `mcp_tool`, such as `update_account`. Finding an operation doesn't run it. If an operation has no `mcp_tool`, none of your listed tools runs it; use the Pylon CLI instead. `call_api_read` and `call_api_write` no longer appear in tool lists, but integrations that already call them by name keep working.

Writes apply immediately and can be visible to customers. Some updates replace a whole list, such as an account's tags, so read the current value first and send the full list. Writes have no idempotency key: if a write's outcome is unknown, read the record before retrying.

...

Some REST API operations aren't available through MCP. ... They're experimental and can change or be removed without notice.

...

Use `error.code` to handle a classified failure. When available, `error` also includes the tool name (`tool`), request identifier (`request_id`), API operation (`operation_id`), HTTP `status`, affected `fields`, or `retry_after_seconds`. ... JSON-RPC errors, including native tool throttling, use their existing format.

### Rate limits

Rate limits are applied per tool and per organization to keep the MCP server healthy under bursty AI traffic. Tool throttling returns a JSON-RPC error with code `-32000`. Its message identifies the tool and tells you how many seconds to wait before retrying. Wait for that delay before retrying the call.

mcp.title: How do I connect to the Pylon MCP Server? | Pylon Knowledge Base
highlights:
The Pylon MCP server at https://mcp.usepylon.com provides AI tools access to your Pylon data. The endpoint uses HTTPS, so the connection is protected with TLS. It uses OAuth authentication with your Pylon account.

The application you connect to Pylon's MCP will only have access to data you would have access to in Pylon, and will read and write on behalf of you.

## Common Clients

### Claude Code

```plaintext
claude mcp add pylon --transport http https://mcp.usepylon.com/
```

Then, in Claude Code, run the `/mcp` command and select the `pylon` MCP to authenticate.

`--transport http` selects MCP's Streamable HTTP transport and stateless request handling; it does not mean that the connection is unencrypted or uses a plaintext HTTP URL. The Pylon endpoint remains HTTPS/TLS-protected.

### Claude Desktop and Web

In "Admin Settings", add a custom connector named "Pylon" with URL `https://mcp.usepylon.com/`

Leave "OAuth Client ID" and "OAuth Client Secret" blank.

Navigate to "Settings > Connectors" and click the "Connect" button next to the Pylon MCP to authenticate.

...

## Authentication Flow

Note: The Pylon MCP server only supports OAuth authentication. API key authentication is not currently available, which may affect usage in remote environments or platforms that don't support OAuth for remote connections.

Current capabilities: The Pylon MCP server provides access to issues, accounts, and contacts, as well as knowledge base articles and collections, macros, tags, and triggers. Tools for tasks, projects, and account notes require Account Intelligence. Available tools can also vary by organization and tool-specific feature flag. Registering a tool does not mean it will appear or be usable in every organization. All tool calls are also subject to the authenticated user's applicable Pylon permissions.

The MCP server does not currently support fetching notebook block content directly. To use notebook content in external tools like Claude, manually open the Account Overview notebook, copy the rendered text block output, and paste it into your conversation as context.

1. When the MCP client connects, it will open your browser

2. Log in with your Pylon account credentials

3. Authorize the MCP connection

4. The browser will redirect back and complete the OAuth flow

5. Your MCP client is now connected to Pylon!

Headless or bot-only clients: The Pylon MCP server does not currently support API keys, machine-to-machine credentials, or other non-OAuth authentication methods. If your client cannot complete the browser-based OAuth flow, it cannot connect directly to the Pylon MCP server today.

If you need token-based access for a supported integration or automation, use the Pylon REST API instead of MCP. The REST API accepts Bearer API tokens, but that authentication method does not apply to the Pylon MCP server.

## Session Expiry and Reconnecting

OAuth sessions expire periodically. The exact duration varies by MCP client - some sessions last a few hours, others can last several days.

mcp.title: Pylon
highlights:
# Pylon

`Pylon` connects an agent to Pylon's hosted MCP server so it can search, read, create, and update support issues, look up and update accounts, and look up contacts as the signed-in user.

Source

...

accDescr: Inside your agent, the model calls tools of the Pylon capability, prefixed pylon_, and gets their results. Your auth function gives the capability a token for each run. The capability sends tools/call with an OAuth Bearer token to the Pylon MCP server at mcp.usepylon.com, which rejects a Pylon REST API token, and with read_only=True it drops the tools not marked read-only.

...

## Before you start

You need a Pylon Member or Admin seat with the `MCP Access` role; Viewer and Integration users cannot sign in. Pylon MCP takes an OAuth access token. Pylon REST API tokens do not work with it.

Your application gets one by running the standard MCP authorization flow: the server names its authorization server and supports dynamic client registration, so any MCP OAuth client library can sign the user in. Store the token it returns and pass it as `auth` or `PYLON_ACCESS_TOKEN`.

...

## Per-user credentials

`auth` decides which Pylon account each run uses:

`auth`

Account used

Not set, `None`, or `''`

`PYLON_ACCESS_TOKEN`. If that is not set either, creating the agent raises an error.

An access token

That token, for every run.

`'oauth'`

The account you sign in to through the browser. This only works on your own machine.

A function

Called at the start of each run, and can be async. The token it returns is used for that run. If it returns `None` or `''`, that run has no Pylon tools. A function never uses `PYLON_ACCESS_TOKEN`, and must not return `'oauth'`.

...

## Tool names

The agent sees each of the server's tools under the `pylon_` prefix, as in `pylon_<tool>`, so they don't collide with other tools on the agent. Set `tool_prefix` to use a different prefix, or `tool_prefix=None` to keep the names the server gives them.

`read_only` selects tools by what the server marks as read-only, not by name, so the prefix does not change what it keeps.

...

## Tool selection and approval

`read_only=True` gives the agent only the tools that Pylon's server labels as read-only, and leaves out all the others. If Pylon has not labeled its read tools, the agent gets no Pylon tools and emits an `MCPReadOnlyNoToolsWarning`. The token's permissions still decide what the agent can reach.
